Why AI Matters for Education

A teacher with 32 students can conference with each one for about ninety seconds a week, if she skips lunch to do it. That math hasn't changed in decades, no matter how good the teacher is. It's why most students get feedback on their writing days or weeks after they wrote it, by which point they've forgotten what they were trying to say in the first place.

That's the actual case for AI in classrooms — not that it's futuristic, but that it changes the math.

At Georgia State University, an advising chatbot named Pounce texts incoming students about missing financial aid forms and paperwork deadlines — the unglamorous stuff that used to cause thousands of admitted students to quietly never show up in the fall. The university tracked a real drop in that "summer melt" after rolling it out. No new advisors were hired. The chatbot just answered the same fifteen questions, at 11 p.m., as many times as needed.

Khan Academy's Khanmigo does something similar for tutoring: instead of handing a student the answer to a math problem, it asks the next question in the sequence, the way a good tutor would if she had unlimited patience and never got tired of explaining fractions. That's the shift worth paying attention to — not AI replacing teachers, but AI absorbing the repetitive parts of teaching that no single human can scale.

None of this fixes education by itself. A chatbot that answers financial aid questions doesn't touch the cost of tuition. A tutoring tool doesn't fix a classroom with forty kids and one teacher. And the tools available right now are uneven — something that walks a student through algebra cleanly can be nearly useless for grading a persuasive essay, where voice and judgment matter more than a single correct answer.

There's a real risk worth naming too: a student who leans on AI to write instead of think ends up unable to do either without it. The same tool that could close a ninety-second feedback gap could just as easily let someone skip the thinking that feedback was supposed to prompt in the first place.

Still, the reason this matters isn't hype. Grading, reminding, repeating — the unglamorous three-quarters of teaching — are exactly what these systems are good at. Handing that work off frees the part of teaching that actually requires a human in the room: noticing when a kid has gone quiet, deciding which mistake is worth stopping the whole class for, caring whether someone shows up tomorrow.
